suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on Egnyte/similar storage appliance access from VPN gateways combined with: user access at off-hours, geographic impossibility vs. last-seen location, bulk operations, or access from service accounts.

suggestion.title: Microsoft 365 Authentication Through Intermediary Proxy Chain
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attackers using 'Brickstorm proxying features and stolen credentials' to access M365 while blending traffic 'to evade Conditional Access policies.' Proxy-mediated M365 auth is evasion signature.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag M365 sign-in events where source IP routing indicates proxy/relay intermediary, user-agent mismatch from historical baseline, or consecutive logins from geographically impossible locations (esp. correlated to VPN sessions).

suggestion.title: Firewall SSL VPN Credential Creation and Immediate Internal Pivot
suggestion.rationale: Article reveals attacker 'enabled and configured SSL VPN access on the victim's firewall, then connected to internal systems.' VPN account creation followed by same-day/next-day internal access is high-confidence lateral move.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate firewall admin events (VPN user creation, access rule modification) with new internal host connections from that VPN gateway within 48 hours. Especially alertable if new VPN user doesn't match existing naming convention or org structure.

suggestion.title: Non-Windows Reverse Shell on Network Appliances (.NET on NAS, Python on Firewall)
suggestion.rationale: Article states Plenet (.NET reverse shell) deployed to Synology NAS and AgentPSD (Python reverse shell) to firewall. Interpreters/runtimes on appliances without legitimate business use are strongly anomalous.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of dotnet/mono runtime or python interpreter on Synology, pfSense, EdgeRouter, or similar appliances. Monitor for child process spawning, unusual network socket binding, or reverse DNS lookups from appliance context.

suggestion.title: Managed Service Provider Compromise Enabling Customer Lateral Movement
suggestion.rationale: Article documents 'this firewall, like the victim organization's Storage Sync system, had also been compromised at least 18 months earlier' when investigating MSP. MSP → customer pivot is multi-tenant escalation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: In MSP environments, flag when: (a) same IP or service-account credentials used to access both MSP systems and customer networks in same 24-48hr window, (b) customer environment accessed from IPs in MSP IP space outside support hours, (c) simultaneous sessions from MSP admin account to customer and known attacker C2.

suggestion.title: Long-Dwell Persistence Without Daily Activity (18+ Month Beacon Pattern)
suggestion.rationale: Article reveals 'at least 18 months before detection' with periodic access, not daily exploitation. Characteristic of dormant backdoor: infrequent C2 checkins, no malware execution for weeks/months, then sudden activity spike.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline for expected legitimate traffic to appliances (Egnyte, pfSense, Synology). Flag: same external IP contacting multiple internal resources on identical schedule (e.g., every 4 weeks for 5 minutes), recurring WebSocket or HTTP connections with identical packet size/timing, or heartbeat-like DNS queries to same sinkholed domain.

suggestion.title: Serv-U CVE-2026-28318 - POST with Content-Encoding: deflate Header
suggestion.rationale: Article core attack description: 'SolarWinds Serv-U is susceptible to specially crafted POST requests that crash the Serv-U service without authentication using Content-Encoding: deflate.' This is the direct exploitation signature and must be detected at network layer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP POST requests to known Serv-U ports (21, 990, 8080, 443) containing 'Content-Encoding: deflate' header from external/untrusted sources. Single occurrence = reconnaissance; >3 attempts in 5 minutes = exploitation. Correlate POST spikes with Serv-U service crash events.

suggestion.title: Serv-U Service Unexpected Termination or Rapid Restart
suggestion.rationale: Article: vulnerability causes service to 'crash the Serv-U service without authentication.' Service crash is the post-exploitation artifact and sole remedial indicator when network telemetry is unavailable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Serv-U service unexpected stops (Windows Event ID 7034, Linux syslog service termination) unaccompanied by scheduled maintenance or admin action. Establish baseline restart frequency; alert on deviations, especially within 2 hours of suspicious inbound traffic on Serv-U ports.

suggestion.title: Network Reconnaissance Scanning for Serv-U Exposure
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Shodan currently tracks over 12,000 Serv-U servers exposed online.' Attackers enumerate targets via mass scanning. Early detection of scanning behavior targeting Serv-U ports prevents exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect burst scanning toward Serv-U ports (FTP 21, FTPS 990, HTTP/S 8080/443) from single external source across multiple internal assets. Alert on >50 connection attempts per minute to Serv-U service ranges, consistent with Shodan-style enumeration.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable Serv-U Version Inventory Alert for CVE-2026-28318
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'SolarWinds released Serv-U 15.5.4 Hotfix 1 on Thursday to patch this denial-of-service vulnerability' and 'CISA flagged it as exploited in the wild.' All versions <15.5.4 HF1 are exploitable; CISA BOD 22-01 mandates patch by June 19.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query CMDB, EDR inventory, and vulnerability scanners for Serv-U installations with version <15.5.4 HF1. Cross-reference with external exposure datasets (Shodan IPs, Censys scans). Alert on any vulnerable instance; escalate to patch management with June 19 BOD deadline.

suggestion.title: Abnormal HTTP POST Request Volume to Serv-U Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'specially crafted POST requests.' Normal Serv-U operation is file-transfer-centric (FTP/SFTP); HTTP POST is anomalous and indicates exploitation probe.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: If Serv-U listens on HTTP/HTTPS ports, establish baseline POST request volume. Alert on >5x baseline spike within 5-minute window to Serv-U endpoints. Flag for anomalous Content-Encoding, Transfer-Encoding, or atypical User-Agent headers. Correlate timing with service crash logs.

suggestion.title: Detect Unauthenticated POST Requests with Deflate Content-Encoding to Serv-U
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'specially crafted POST requests using the Content-Encoding: deflate header' cause crash. This is the attack vector and should be the primary detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for HTTP POST requests with Content-Encoding: deflate header targeting Serv-U service listening ports (default 22, 3389, or environment-specific). No authentication required per article, so baseline unauthenticated POST volume. Flag any hit as potential exploitation attempt.

suggestion.title: Monitor SolarWinds Serv-U Service Unexpected Termination
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'crash the Serv-U service without authentication.' Unplanned service stops are the observable impact and critical for post-exploitation triage.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on SolarWinds Serv-U process (sshd.exe, SshServer.exe variants) unexpected termination within 5 minutes of HTTP POST traffic. Correlate: POST request → process exit → service restart attempt.

suggestion.title: Asset Inventory: Detect SolarWinds Serv-U Vulnerable Versions Pre-CVE-2026-28318 Patch
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies federal patch due 2026-06-19. Patch-lag detection is critical for CISA KEV entries — compliance auditors will ask. Asset-exposure hunt template should query vulnerability scanner for installed version < patched build.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query vulnerability scanner or CMDB for SolarWinds Serv-U instances. Extract version. Flag instances with version < official patched build as 'exploitable by CVE-2026-28318.' Correlate against observed POST traffic to exposed instances.

suggestion.title: Detect HTTP 50x Errors from Serv-U Following POST Requests with Deflate Encoding
suggestion.rationale: Resource exhaustion and crashes manifest as 500-series HTTP errors. Article describes DoS; HTTP error spike is the secondary observable that confirms exploitation success.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Spike detection on HTTP 50x responses from Serv-U endpoints. Correlate with: (a) prior POST requests with Content-Encoding: deflate, (b) absence of legitimate user traffic patterns, (c) service restart logs within 2 minutes.

suggestion.title: Detect Serv-U Port Scanning and Enumeration Preceding Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Attackers must identify exposed Serv-U to exploit. Article emphasizes 'public-facing application' — reconnaissance for open Serv-U ports (22, 3389, custom ranges) precedes the exploit.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for port-scan or service-enumeration traffic to Serv-U listening ports from external/untrusted subnets. Flag SYN-flood-like patterns or OS fingerprinting attempts. Chain: scan → version discovery (banner grab) → POST exploit.

suggestion.title: Suspicious File Upload to Cisco SD-WAN Manager
suggestion.rationale: Article states attacker 'could exploit this vulnerability by uploading a crafted file to the affected system' with Mandiant observing actual exploitation attempts uploading malicious configuration files.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager for unusual file upload activity, particularly .csv uploads to /home/admin/ or similar directories. Baseline normal administrative file operations and alert on uploads from unexpected network segments or outside business hours.

suggestion.title: Command Injection in vScript Processing
suggestion.rationale: Article describes vulnerability as 'insufficient validation of user-supplied input' enabling 'command injection attacks' through vScript processing of uploaded files.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor /var/log/scripts.log for suspicious vScript command execution patterns. Alert on invocations of vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh with unexpected arguments or file paths, particularly malicious.csv or suspicious .csv files from non-standard directories.

suggestion.title: Netadmin to Root Privilege Escalation on SD-WAN Manager
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states vulnerability 'allow local attackers with low privileges to execute arbitrary commands as root' and requires 'netadmin privileges' as prerequisite, describing direct escalation path.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect privilege escalation from netadmin user context to root execution. Monitor for processes spawned by netadmin that execute system binaries typically reserved for root, or for setuid/sudo abuse patterns involving /usr/bin/vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh.

suggestion.title: Chained Authentication Bypass to Netadmin Account Exploitation (CVE-2026-20182/127)
suggestion.rationale: Article states netadmin privileges required and notes 'This would require valid credentials or exploitation of CVE-2026-20182 or CVE-2026-20127', describing a multi-stage authentication bypass chain.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate authentication bypass attempt logs (from CVE-2026-20182 and CVE-2026-20127 exploitation patterns) followed within hours by netadmin account creation, credential modification, or privilege assignment, then suspicious file upload activity to SD-WAN Manager.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Tenant Configuration Upload via vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh
suggestion.rationale: Mandiant IOC explicitly mentions 'upload tenant configuration data to vSmart controllers' with example showing vScript execution of vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh with malicious .csv file path argument.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor /var/log/scripts.log for vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh execution with suspicious command-line arguments (e.g., '-cli path /home/admin/malicious.csv vpn 0'). Alert on configuration uploads from unexpected netadmin accounts or involving file paths containing suspicious CSV file names.

suggestion.title: Bulk Malicious Configuration Deployment to Catalyst Edge Devices
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'limited cases where the exploitation of this bug resulted in a configuration change pushed to edge devices', indicating lateral movement to interconnected SD-WAN network containing up to 6,000 managed devices.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect abnormal bulk configuration pushes from SD-WAN Manager to large numbers of edge devices. Alert on configuration changes occurring outside scheduled maintenance windows, from unexpected administrator accounts, or affecting 50+ devices simultaneously with unusual vSmart controller serial number patterns.

suggestion.title: FIFA World Cup Phishing Domain Registration
suggestion.rationale: Article title mentions 'Fake Sites' as primary attack vector. Pipeline failed to extract lookalike domain indicators or registration patterns that would enable proactive detection of counterfeit FIFA portals.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect newly registered domains containing 'fifa', 'world cup 2026' or common misspellings (fifaa, fifa2026, etc.) registered to bulletproof hosters or privacy services. Correlate with phishing link URLs in email or web proxy logs.

suggestion.title: Banking Malware C2 Communication
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names 'Banking Malware' as attack component. Pipeline extracted no network IOCs, file hashes, or C2 indicators despite this being core to the threat.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for outbound HTTPS traffic from desktop endpoints to non-standard ports or encrypted channels exhibiting characteristics of banking malware (beaconing patterns, suspicious TLS certificates, known malware C2 domains/IPs).

suggestion.title: Web Form Credential Harvesting via Fake Ticketing Portal
suggestion.rationale: Article title includes 'Stolen Logins'—pipeline failed to surface detection for form-hijacking, HTML injection, or keylogging patterns typical of fake ticketing/registration portals.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect browser processes spawning unusual child processes (clipboarders, keystroke loggers) or suspicious DLL injections during credential entry. Flag DOM changes indicating form interception on FIFA-themed URLs.

suggestion.title: Malware Persistence via Browser Extension or Startup
suggestion.rationale: Banking malware requires persistence post-execution. Article mentions malware delivery but pipeline did not map persistence techniques commonly deployed by eCrime actors in credential-theft campaigns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unsigned browser extensions installed to %AppData% during execution window of phishing payloads, or suspicious Registry modifications in Run/RunOnce keys with obfuscated paths post-malware delivery.

suggestion.title: Compromised Credential Usage Against Banking Portals
suggestion.rationale: Stolen logins are useless without exploitation. Pipeline did not generate detection for lateral movement or account takeover using harvested credentials against financial institutions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag sign-ins from phishing site geolocation or TOR IPs using credentials harvested from FIFA scam campaign. Correlate failed authentication attempts followed by successful login within short window, indicating credential spray.

suggestion.title: DbGate POST /runners/start HTTP endpoint exploitation attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'POST /runners/start allows remote code execution' and 'The functionName value is interpolated directly into dynamically generated JavaScript source code.' Any HTTP POST to /runners/start is an exploitation attempt by definition.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on any POST request to endpoints containing /runners/start or /runners/load-reader. Baseline legitimate usage if DbGate is deployed; flag all others as exploitation. HTTP 200/201 response from these endpoints is high-fidelity signal. Inspect JSON body for functionName parameter containing shell metacharacters, backticks, $(), process.spawn, require, or eval patterns.

suggestion.title: DbGate JavaScript code-injection via functionName parameter inspection
suggestion.rationale: Article core mechanism: 'The functionName value is interpolated directly into dynamically generated JavaScript source code via string concatenation.' Pipeline must detect anomalous functionName payloads in POST /runners/start requests.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Parse JSON body of POST /runners/start requests. Extract functionName field. Flag if value deviates from expected format (simple alphanumeric identifiers) or contains code patterns (backticks, $(), require, child_process, spawn, exec, eval). Whitelist known-good function names to reduce false positives.

suggestion.title: DbGate Node.js spawning unexpected child processes post-injection
suggestion.rationale: Article: code 'executed in a forked Node.js child process.' Detection in UC_26_2 is process-centric; this adds correlation with web traffic—Node.js spawning shell utilities AFTER a POST /runners/start request.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate HTTP POST to /runners/start (from web logs) with Node.js child-process spawning within 2 seconds. Flag if child is a shell (sh, bash, powershell) or utilities (curl, wget, nc, python) not expected in DbGate's normal operation. Parent process command-line should contain 'bundle.js' or '.dbgate'.

suggestion.title: DbGate file-system write post-code execution (persistence or payload staging)
suggestion.rationale: Article describes code execution in Node.js; attackers may stage payloads, write persistence mechanisms, or modify binaries. Detection should monitor file writes from Node.js processes matching DbGate patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor file creation/modification events where InitiatingProcessFileName is node/node.exe with command-line containing 'bundle.js' or '.dbgate'. Alert on writes to sensitive directories (/usr/bin, /usr/local/bin, /etc, /root/.ssh, /tmp with x permissions). Baseline expected writes and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: DbGate unauthenticated endpoint access pattern (T1190 initial foothold)
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes vulnerability is 'unauthenticated.' Any access to /runners/start or /runners/load-reader without prior authentication session/token is exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Extract POST requests to /runners/start. Cross-reference source IP against active authenticated sessions in application logs. Flag POST requests from IPs with no prior successful /auth/login or token grant within preceding 5 minutes as unauthenticated exploitation attempts.

suggestion.title: DbGate: Unauthenticated JWT token issuance from /auth/login (T1078 abuse)
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'the none auth provider issues JWT tokens without credentials via POST /auth/login' — this is the attack enabler. Any /auth/login request that returns a JWT without credential validation is exploitable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect POST to */auth/login endpoints returning HTTP 200 with JWT/Bearer tokens in response body when no Authorization header or authentication credentials were present in request. Alert on 'none' auth provider being active in DbGate configuration.

suggestion.title: DbGate: ZIP file upload followed by unzipDirectory() invocation (T1204.002 + T1505.003)
suggestion.rationale: Article describes uploading 'a malicious ZIP with ../ entries' that then gets extracted via unzipDirectory(). T1204.002 is the user-supplied malicious file; T1505.003 is writing the extracted payload to system paths. These should be detected as a correlated sequence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate POST to */api/archive/upload or */api/archive/save-uploaded-zip with ZIP file name in request body, followed within 5 seconds by POST to */api/archive/unzip from same source IP. Flag ZIPs with path-traversal patterns (..) if available in file inspection.

suggestion.title: DbGate: Writes to /etc/ld.so.preload by node process (T1505.003 library hijacking)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly lists '/etc/ld.so.preload' as a write target. This is a high-severity persistence mechanism (library preloading for code injection). Warrants standalone detection due to rarity and severity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on any write (create or modify) to /etc/ld.so.preload. This file is rarely modified in production and has near-zero legitimate use cases. Immediate escalation recommended.

suggestion.title: DbGate: Root-context node process writing to system-critical paths (privilege escalation indicator)
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'DbGate runs as root' in default Docker deployment. Combination of (process=node UID=0) + (writes to /etc/, /root/, /var/spool/) outside normal application directories is direct RCE evidence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate node process running with UID=0 (root) with file write events to /etc/*, /root/*, or /var/spool/* outside /app or /home/dbgate directories. The presence of root UID on node + system-path writes is abnormal and indicates successful privilege abuse.

suggestion.title: DbGate: Writes to multiple cron systems in short timespan (T1053.003 multi-vector persistence)
suggestion.rationale: Article lists cron.d, cron.daily, cron.hourly, cron.weekly, cron.monthly, and /var/spool/cron as write targets. Attacker writes to multiple cron locations to ensure persistence. Single write to one cron location could be legitimate, but writes to 2+ cron systems indicates attempted persistence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when a single process writes to 2 or more of: /etc/cron.d/, /etc/cron.daily/, /etc/cron.weekly/, /etc/cron.monthly/, /var/spool/cron/ within a 10-second window. Multi-target cron writes are rare in legitimate operations and strongly indicate persistence installation.

suggestion.title: DbGate: Sequential unauthenticated API exploitation chain (T1190 → T1078 → T1204.002 → T1505.003)
suggestion.rationale: Article's kill chain is: no-auth login → token issuance → ZIP upload → unzip execution → file write to system paths. Detecting the full sequence with timing constraints and source-IP consistency is highest fidelity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect 4-step sequence from same IP: (1) POST /auth/login returns 200 + JWT, no prior auth, (2) POST /api/archive/upload or /api/archive/save-uploaded-zip with ZIP file <5s after login, (3) POST /api/archive/unzip <5s after upload, (4) DeviceFileEvents show node writing to /etc/*, /root/*, or /var/spool/* within 10s of unzip call. End-to-end timing <30s indicates exploitation.

suggestion.title: DbGate authenticated /runners/load-reader POST with code-injection keywords
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Any user with valid DbGate credentials can execute arbitrary OS commands'. Current UC_24_2 detects injection keywords but does not emphasize the requirement for HTTP 200 (success) status combined with suspicious parameters. Missing hunt for successful exploitation attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: POST /runners/load-reader with HTTP 200 response, where the request URL or body contains functionName parameter with code-injection patterns (import(, child_process, execSync, eval). Authenticated users only. Cross-correlate with post-exploitation shell-spawning (UC_24_3) for confirmation.

suggestion.title: DbGate dynamic import() bypass exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly notes: 'The require = null mitigation is trivially bypassed via dynamic import()'. This is the specific exploitation technique. Current hunts check for import() generically; this hunt targets the bypass pattern directly.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: POST /runners/load-reader where the request contains 'import(' preceded by async/await or in a promise context. The bypass works because import() is async and eval() is not; signatures should look for async function definitions or import() calls within functionName parameter values.

suggestion.title: DbGate root-level shell process privilege escalation
suggestion.rationale: Article states RCE executes 'as root'—critical detail. UC_24_3 detects shell-spawning from node but does not verify privilege escalation. Should detect when a non-root node process spawns shells running as uid=0 or SYSTEM.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Shell process (bash, sh, cmd.exe, powershell.exe) spawned from node/dbgate where the parent process AccountName is not SYSTEM/root but the child process runs as SYSTEM/uid=0. This indicates privilege escalation via code-injection RCE.

suggestion.title: DbGate application log errors in loadReader handler
suggestion.rationale: No hunt currently covers application-level telemetry. Article describes code-injection into JavaScript execution; DbGate app logs would emit SyntaxError or ReferenceError when processing malicious functionName values.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search DbGate application logs for exceptions or parse errors in the /runners/load-reader handler or loadReader function. Keywords: SyntaxError, ReferenceError, 'import', 'spawn', 'exec'. Volume spike in errors on this endpoint is suspicious.

suggestion.title: DbGate file/directory discovery post-exploitation
suggestion.rationale: RCE as root would enable attackers to enumerate files and directories. Article does not mention specific post-exploitation IOCs, but ls/dir commands spawned from the compromised node process under root privileges would be typical follow-on behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Child processes spawned from node/dbgate running as root executing ls, find, dir, Get-ChildItem, or similar discovery commands. Particularly suspicious if followed by credential file access (/etc/passwd, /root/.ssh, /etc/shadow) or config file enumeration.

suggestion.title: ait-bsc file write to unexpected log directories via path traversal
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'arbitrary filesystem paths' and 'bypass the configured log root.' Detection must identify files written outside /var/opt/ait-bsc/logs or equivalent known-good paths.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor ait-bsc process (pid, parent) creating or modifying files in unexpected directories (/etc/, /home/, /tmp/, /root/, /usr/bin/, /usr/local/bin/, cron.d, systemd service dirs). Anomalous activity when ait-bsc spawns file operations outside its configured log root is high-signal.

suggestion.title: Unauthenticated access to ait-bsc BSC HTTP API without authentication headers
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'unauthenticated HTTP API for dynamically creating packet capture handlers.' Basic baseline detection: HTTP requests to /*/start endpoints lacking auth tokens/session cookies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: POST requests to ait-bsc /*/start endpoint (any handler name) originating from non-internal IP ranges and missing Authorization header, X-API-Key, or session cookie. High confidence if combined with path-traversal payloads in form data.

suggestion.title: Python interpreter or shell spawned by ait-bsc process
suggestion.rationale: If attacker writes malicious .py or shell script via path traversal and ait-bsc or scheduled task executes it, spawning python/bash from ait-bsc parent is an execution indicator of successful exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Child process creation events where parent is ait-bsc (python, bash, sh, or any interpreter) with suspicious command-line arguments (curl, wget, nc, reverse shell patterns). ait-bsc is not expected to spawn interpreters in normal operation.

suggestion.title: Executable or script staging in world-writable directories by ait-bsc
suggestion.rationale: Post-exploitation, attacker may write binaries to /tmp, /var/tmp, or other writable locations for later execution. Direct file-write detection from ait-bsc to these paths.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: ait-bsc process creating executable files (.py, .sh, ELF binaries) in /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, or other commonly-abused staging directories. Confidence elevated if accompanied by subsequent execution or cron/systemd modifications.

suggestion.title: Modification of cron, systemd, or init.d scripts by ait-bsc or during ait-bsc runtime window
suggestion.rationale: Path traversal allows write to /etc/cron.d/, /etc/systemd/system/, /etc/init.d/. These are persistence vectors post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: File creation or modification in /etc/cron.d/, /etc/crontab, /etc/systemd/system/, /lib/systemd/system/, /etc/init.d/ with timestamp coinciding with or shortly after inbound ait-bsc HTTP requests or ait-bsc process activity.

suggestion.title: ait-bsc config or environment file poisoning
suggestion.rationale: If attacker writes to bsc.yaml, config files, or Python site-packages (mentioned in article's ait-venv paths), next restart/import may execute attacker code. Monitor for writes to these sensitive locations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: File creation/modification in ait installation directories (./ait-venv/lib/python*/site-packages/ait/, /etc/ait/, /opt/ait/) or bsc configuration files (bsc.yaml, StreamCaptureManager configs) by processes other than package managers or scheduled deployments.

suggestion.title: HTTP POST/PUT/PATCH to Shopper Team Settings Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly details exploitation of unprotected `/settings/team/index` and `/settings/team/role-permission` endpoints. UC_13_1 in article demonstrates expected detection; pipeline failed to generate.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor POST/PUT/PATCH requests to /settings/team/*, /livewire/update, /livewire/message/settings.team from any authenticated user. Cross-reference user privilege level: alert if low-privilege accounts access these endpoints. Implement Splunk CIM-based detection per article's UC_13_1 SPL; replace generic Defender KQL with custom HTTP ingestion since M365 XDR cannot natively monitor self-hosted PHP application traffic.

suggestion.title: RBAC Role Creation and Admin User Deletion Events
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers could 'create new roles and delete other users, including administrators.' This exploitation impact must trigger on application RBAC audit logs, not just HTTP monitoring.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on role creation events and user account deletions in application audit logs. Flag when initiated by users with insufficient privilege to perform RBAC changes. Correlate with suspicious HTTP access to /settings/team/* within 5-minute window. Specifically flag deletion of accounts with admin or elevated directory roles.

suggestion.title: Shopper Application Vulnerability Asset Exposure
suggestion.rationale: Article 'Why this matters' section explicitly references '2 use case(s) fired'—second is asset exposure template per canonical detection. Must identify Shopper instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-47744.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query asset/application inventory and vulnerability scanner output for Shopper product running vulnerable versions of affected components. Prioritize instances with internet exposure or accessibility from non-administrative networks. Cross-reference with business criticality to triage.

suggestion.title: Everest Forms Pro Plugin Exploit Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states 'hackers exploit critical Everest Forms Pro WordPress plugin flaw to take over sites.' No detection UC was generated despite this being the core attack vector. Title establishes exploitation as the initial access method.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP requests targeting Everest Forms Pro endpoints known to contain remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities. Flag requests with suspicious parameters, encoded payloads, or POST requests to form submission handlers from unfamiliar sources.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Shell Write Detection on WordPress
suggestion.rationale: Title phrase 'take over sites' implies file write and execution capability. No detection for post-exploit persistence (webshells, backdoors) was generated despite this being the likely outcome of WordPress site takeover.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect suspicious file writes to WordPress directories (wp-content, wp-plugins, wp-admin) immediately following successful exploit attempts, particularly PHP or executable files with obfuscated names. Correlate with HTTP 200 responses from file paths that should not exist.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Plugin Installation/Update Activity
suggestion.rationale: Site takeover implies attacker may install malicious plugins or modify existing ones. Article does not discuss post-compromise persistence mechanisms, but this is a standard WordPress attack follow-up absent from use case generation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor WordPress plugin directories for unauthorized or unexpected plugin installations, particularly by non-administrative processes. Flag rapid plugin updates or installation of plugins with generic names during suspicious time windows.

suggestion.title: WordPress Database Access from Suspicious Processes
suggestion.rationale: Site takeover requires database access for credential theft or admin account creation. No detection for unusual database connections from compromised application context was proposed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect database connections to WordPress databases (wp_users, wp_posts tables) from web application processes or unusual parent processes. Flag bulk SELECT queries on user credential tables or INSERT operations creating new admin accounts.

suggestion.title: Malicious PyPI Package Installed via Hash Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly provides SHA1 hash (a01c2a21f24db63cb01a67016519aebeca438089) and recommends 'File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match' as a hunt template. Pipeline generated zero use cases despite this directive.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for file creation/execution matching SHA1 a01c2a21f24db63cb01a67016519aebeca438089 on endpoints. Alert if this hash appears in process execution, library import, or installed package directory (site-packages/). Correlate with Python interpreter activity.

suggestion.title: Typosquatted Python Package Installation Detection
suggestion.rationale: Core attack vector: legitimate 'parsimonious' mimicked by malicious 'parsimonius' (one-letter substitution). Article: 'The package...was crafted to look almost identical...The single missing letter was no [...]'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Python package installations via pip. Flag packages with names differing from legitimate libraries by single character edits (Levenshtein distance ≤1). Alert specifically on 'parsimonius' or similar typosquatted variants of known parsers.

suggestion.title: Anomalous PyPI Package Metadata Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states malicious package 'quietly made its way into PyPI repository'—implies detection should catch newly published packages with suspicious metadata or mismatched provenance compared to legitimate originals.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag pip install requests for recently-created packages with metadata mismatches (different author, description, or suspicious dependencies). Cross-reference PyPI metadata for anomalies: new registration date, no version history, minimal package size.

suggestion.title: Hola Browser Setup Spawns me.exe Child Process
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states malicious executable 'named me.exe' was 'distributing alongside its legitimate installer.' Pipeline should generate composite detection correlating Hola installer execution (setup.exe) with me.exe spawning, not generic installer → cmd/powershell. This captures the specific supply-chain payload delivery.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when Hola Browser installer (setup.exe, update.exe, or msi-based process) spawns or creates me.exe as a child process, or both appear in the same temp/AppData directory within 60 seconds. Supply-chain context: official installer from compromised delivery pipeline.

suggestion.title: me.exe Execution with CPU/Memory Spike (Cryptominer Behavioral)
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies payload as 'Cryptominer' but pipeline contains no impact-phase hunt. Cryptominers characteristically consume sustained CPU/GPU resources. Article phrase: 'distributing...Cryptominer' establishes the expected behavior post-infection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate me.exe process creation with elevated and sustained CPU usage (>50% for >10 minutes) or GPU utilization on the same endpoint. Cryptominers often spawn multiple child processes (stratum workers, pool connection processes) to maximize resource theft.

suggestion.title: me.exe Binary Code Signature Mismatch or Unsigned
suggestion.rationale: Single-character executable name (me.exe) distributed via compromised supply chain is highly suspicious. Article does not confirm signing status, but the artifact's unusual name and delivery method (embedded in legitimate installer) suggest unsigned or mismatched signing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of me.exe with missing Authenticode signature, unsigned status, or signature issuer not matching expected Hola/parent company identity. Context: supply-chain compromise means official signature chain is compromised; unsigned or third-party signature indicates post-compromise modification.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Package Publishing (account anomaly)
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attack via npm requires malicious package upload. Article describes compromised-package distribution but pipeline extracted zero initial-access detections. Cite: title 'Hit npm in Supply Chain Attacks'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm registry API calls and web UI logins for account anomalies preceding package publication: unusual login geographies, MFA disable, API key generation from new devices, rapid successive package uploads from low-volume developers.

suggestion.title: Code Execution from npm install (postinstall script)
suggestion.rationale: npm supply-chain malware executes at install time via lifecycle scripts. Pipeline did not surface execution-phase detections. Cite: implicit in supply-chain attack model.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect spawning of shell or system processes (cmd.exe, powershell, sh, bash) from npm.exe or node.exe contexts during package installation. Flag postinstall/preinstall hooks, native module builds, and process execution from node_modules/.bin paths with unexpected parent chains.

suggestion.title: C2 Beaconing from npm-Installed Malware
suggestion.rationale: Miasma and IronWorm variants must exfiltrate or receive commands post-execution. Pipeline generated zero C2-detection or exfiltration use cases. Cite: threat-actor names imply active post-compromise behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound network connections from node.exe or npm-spawned child processes to non-standard ports or newly-registered domains. Baseline expected CDN and registry traffic; flag deviations. Cross-reference against known malware C2 infrastructure tied to IronWorm and Miasma.

suggestion.title: Package Name Confusion / Typosquatting Detection
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain npm attacks often exploit name similarity ('Miasma variant' suggests obfuscated naming). Pipeline did not extract masquerading or initial-access detections. Cite: 'New Miasma Worm Variant' and npm's well-known typosquatting risk.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install logs and node_modules directory for packages with names similar to popular libraries (Levenshtein distance, unicode homoglyph substitution). Flag packages published by unfamiliar maintainers, with zero or single-digit download counts, or publishing after dormancy.

suggestion.title: Persistence via package.json Script Injection
suggestion.rationale: Malware variants persist via preinstall/postinstall hooks or by injecting initialization code. Pipeline did not generate persistence-phase detections. Cite: standard supply-chain persistence mechanism in npm ecosystem.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect suspicious or obfuscated script content in package.json lifecycle hooks (preinstall, postinstall, prepare). Monitor for file modifications to installed node_modules that introduce require() hooks, environment variable exfiltration, or wrapper code targeting application initialization paths.

suggestion.title: Sensitive Data Exfiltration from Affected Applications
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain malware exfiltrates source code, environment variables, or application data. Pipeline did not surface impact-phase or exfiltration detections. Cite: inherent impact of compromised npm packages used in production.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual outbound data transfer volume from application servers to external IPs on non-standard ports. Correlate process chains originating from node.exe or npm contexts with file-access events targeting .env, config files, or source code directories. Flag connections to infrastructure linked to IronWorm or Miasma operators.

suggestion.title: DD-WRT UPnP Stack Overflow Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'stack buffer overflow flaw in the UPnP service of affected routers, letting attackers gain full access without any credentials.' This is the initial access vector but no execution-phase detection was generated. Need behavioral/network-based detection for exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DD-WRT router UPnP services (UDP 1900, TCP 49152-49161) for malformed or oversized requests targeting buffer boundaries. Spike in failed UPnP service responses followed by successful shell access indicates exploitation attempt. Correlate with C0XMO signatures if available.

suggestion.title: Gafgyt/C0XMO Bot Command Execution on Compromised Routers
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'modular propagation' and targets 'multiple Linux architectures'—strongly implies post-exploitation command execution on compromised devices. T1059 is conspicuously missing despite being the core malware behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for unusual shell spawning from UPnP daemons, busybox/sh execution from non-standard paths on Linux routers, or shell commands downloading files from attacker IPs. Watch for wget/curl to C0XMO C2 addresses from router-level processes.

suggestion.title: C0XMO Multi-Architecture Binary Download & Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'targets multiple Linux architectures' with 'modular propagation'—indicates downloading and executing binaries for ARM, x86, MIPS, PowerPC architectures. T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer) and persistence mechanisms entirely missing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect file downloads to /tmp or /var/tmp from listed C2 IPs (85.215.131.70, 217.160.125.125, 176.100.37.91) followed by chmod +x and execution. Flag binary files with multiple ELF headers (ARM, MIPS, x86) downloaded in succession—hallmark of architecture-agnostic botnet propagation.

suggestion.title: Network Propagation Scanning for New Vulnerable Targets
suggestion.rationale: The phrase 'modular propagation' and botnet targeting 'multiple devices' implies active network scanning for DD-WRT instances. T1046 (Network Service Discovery) or T1595 (Active Scanning) should be detected but are absent.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify infected routers performing UPnP scanning on internal/external networks (probing UDP 1900, TCP 49152 ranges). Correlate scanning source IPs with later C0XMO hash execution. Watch for Shodan-like reconnaissance queries (HTTP 'User-Agent' containing scanner signatures).

suggestion.title: C2 Callback Detection from Linux IoT Devices
suggestion.rationale: Three C2 IPs provided (85.215.131.70, 217.160.125.125, 176.100.37.91) but pipeline generated no corresponding network-based hunt. This is a basic, high-fidelity IOC that should drive immediate detection rules.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on any outbound TCP/UDP connections from non-standard ports on Linux devices (especially routers, IoT) to 85.215.131.70, 217.160.125.125, or 176.100.37.91. Pair with process execution chain from UPnP/bot agent. Flag persistent, periodic beaconing patterns consistent with botnet C2 heartbeat.

suggestion.title: Stripe Webhook Abuse for C2 Communication
suggestion.rationale: Article states Stripe functions as 'both its command center and its data dump'—explicit evidence of malware using payment processor webhooks and APIs as C2 infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unusual Stripe API calls (webhook creation, updates to endpoints), rapid sequential API calls from non-standard merchant accounts, and HTTP POST/PUT traffic to payment processor infrastructure from suspected malware execution context.

suggestion.title: Credit Card Data Exfiltration via Payment Processor Account
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'credit card skimming malware' routing stolen card data to Stripe as 'data dump'—bulk token operations and non-standard exfiltration patterns via trusted payment service.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect abnormal volume of payment token creation outside baseline, suspicious Stripe API authentication from non-whitelisted accounts, and correlate bulk card operations with malware command timing indicators.

suggestion.title: Malicious Script Injection into Payment Forms
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware is 'hiding inside one of the most trusted payment platforms'—indicates web-based code injection into payment processing pages, core Magecart technique.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for unexpected or unsigned JavaScript loading in payment form context, anomalous DOM manipulation targeting card input fields, and network callbacks from injected scripts to attacker-controlled or suspicious domains.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Compromise Leveraging Payment Processor Trust
suggestion.rationale: Attack explicitly weaponizes Stripe's trusted status in e-commerce ecosystem, using legitimate payment infrastructure as both attack vector and operational relay—classic third-party trust abuse.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unauthorized Stripe integration changes, new webhook registrations pointing to suspicious endpoints, API key generation from unexpected sources, and suspicious subdomains mimicking legitimate payment processor URLs.

suggestion.title: IIS Web Shell File Creation
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Custom Web Shell Framework' targets IIS servers — this is persistence via file write. Pipeline generated zero persistence detections despite clear attack narrative.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on creation/modification of .asp, .aspx, .php, .jsp files in C:\inetpub\wwwroot or web app directories. Combine with file content analysis (obfuscation, encoding) and cross-reference with unusual w3wp.exe activity. High fidelity if created outside normal deployment processes.

suggestion.title: IIS Worker Process Command Spawning
suggestion.rationale: Web shell execution occurs via w3wp.exe spawning interpreters (cmd.exe, powershell.exe). Title indicates 'custom framework' — implies operator control via web shell, requiring command execution detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag w3wp.exe parent spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or cscript.exe with network connections. Baseline IIS process trees and alert on unexpected child processes, especially with network activity to external IPs.

suggestion.title: HTTP C2 Beacon Pattern Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'custom web shell framework' — implies coded protocol for operator communication. Pipeline missed HTTP-layer detection for C2 interaction phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor IIS logs for unusual access patterns to recently created .asp/.aspx endpoints: high request frequency from single source, large request/response bodies, non-browser User-Agents, unusual HTTP methods (PUT, TRACE). Correlate with w3wp.exe execution spikes.

suggestion.title: OP-512 Threat Actor Reputation Check
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly names 'Threat Cluster OP-512' — threat actor identifier must be enriched against past incidents, known C2 infrastructure, and public IOC feeds.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Ingest OP-512 historical IOCs from public reporting. Monitor for DNS/IP connections to previously attributed C2, attacker infrastructure, or phishing domains. Block on network edge if advisable; alert on internal DNS queries to known OP-512 domains.

suggestion.title: IIS Module and Handler Injection
suggestion.rationale: Custom framework may persist via IIS modules (T1505.004) rather than simple shell file. Pipeline did not generate IIS configuration abuse detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for appcmd.exe execution or direct applicationHost.config modifications. Alert on new handler mappings, module installations, or application pool changes. Baseline and audit all IIS module additions; flag unsigned or non-Microsoft modules.

suggestion.title: SMTP Relay Software Installed on Cloud Compute Instances
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly describes SMTP relay operation as primary attack objective—'Hijacks 230 AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure Servers for Covert SMTP Relay Network'—yet pipeline generated zero detections for this core impact. Attackers must have installed/configured mail transport agents (postfix, sendmail, exim) on compromised instances.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor process execution and package installation events for mail relay software (sendmail, postfix, exim, qmail) on cloud compute instances lacking baseline mail-server role. Alert on service startup for mail daemons. Correlate package install logs with account creation timelines to establish persistence mechanism.

suggestion.title: High-Volume Outbound SMTP from Cloud Instances
suggestion.rationale: Operating 230-instance relay network implies measurable SMTP traffic signature. Pipeline failed to generate detection for abuse of cloud infrastructure for malicious SMTP operations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outbound SMTP connections (ports 25, 587, 465) from cloud instances to non-cloud SMTP servers or high-volume transmission patterns (>1000 emails/hour). Baseline mail relay instances and alert on deviations. Correlate with DNS queries for mail relay infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Cloud Account Creation and API Privilege Escalation
suggestion.rationale: Maintaining control over 230 instances requires persistence; attackers likely created service accounts with infrastructure-modification privileges. Article implies account manipulation but pipeline generated no detection for cloud account lifecycle anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor service account creation with elevated IAM roles (Compute Admin, Owner equivalent). Alert on human-initiated account creation outside standard provisioning workflows. Correlate new service accounts with subsequent infrastructure modifications or API calls to instances later identified as compromised.

suggestion.title: Bulk Cloud Infrastructure Reconnaissance and Enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Identifying and compromising 230 instances across three cloud providers requires systematic discovery. Pipeline missed detection for cloud infrastructure scanning (DescribeInstances, ListInstances, List operations).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect bulk cloud instance enumeration APIs (DescribeInstances, ListInstances, ListVMs) executed by single principal in compressed time window. Alert on enum operations followed by instance access/modification attempts. Correlate with geographically anomalous authentication locations.

suggestion.title: Cloud Security Group / Network ACL Modifications Enabling SMTP Egress
suggestion.rationale: Outbound SMTP relay requires network rule modifications at scale. Article establishes 230-instance scope implying bulk infrastructure changes. Pipeline generated no detection for network defense evasion.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor security group/NSG/firewall rule creation/modification allowing outbound SMTP (25, 587, 465) from compute instances. Alert on rules created by non-standard service principals or after-hours. Correlate rule changes with subsequent SMTP traffic or mail relay software installation.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Cloud API Authentication from Leaked or Brute-Forced Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Initial compromise vector for 230 instances across three providers must involve credential compromise or exploitation. Pipeline generated no detection for credential-access or initial-access attack phases.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor failed API authentication attempts followed by successful login from same principal from anomalous geolocation. Alert on API activity inconsistent with baseline (bulk operations from new service account, operations from credential-exposed git repository). Correlate with known credential dumps.

suggestion.title: HTTP 401 Authentication Prompt from External CDN Domain
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes the attack mechanism: 'starting in late May 2026, the polyfill[.]io domain became active again and started responding with HTTP 401 authentication requests. User browsers visiting pages such as Toshiba's and MUJI's interpret that as a request for a username and password, so they serve a login prompt.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP 401 responses from external third-party domains loaded in script/link tags on customer-facing websites. Correlate with known-compromised CDN domains (polyfill.io). Alert on authentication challenges from domains outside the primary SaaS provider's owned infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Stale Malicious Dependency References in Production Code
suggestion.rationale: Article notes the root cause: 'some sites using the service failed to clean all their pages over the past two years, so remnants of Polyfill code remained.' This cleanup failure enabled re-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan production web applications for hardcoded references to polyfill.io or other known-compromised CDN domains. Flag any references not updated to polyfill.top or removed. Compare deployed code inventory against vulnerability advisories for supply-chain incidents.

suggestion.title: Re-Registration of Dormant Malicious Domain with HTTP 401 Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Temporal shift in domain behavior: 'While the deactivation of the service at polyfill[.]io stopped the redirections...starting in late May 2026, the polyfill[.]io domain became active again.' Domain re-emergence with authentication challenge responses is a distinct signal.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor WHOIS changes and DNS re-activation for domains previously linked to supply-chain incidents. Alert when a dormant domain begins responding with unusual HTTP status codes (especially 401, 403). Correlate re-activation with spike in browser authentication prompts on dependent websites.

suggestion.title: Credential Submission Following Visit to Compromised Third-Party Website
suggestion.rationale: Attack success metric stated in article: 'Users who entered their account login data in the authentication screens' and Toshiba's guidance 'if you do see it, please select Cancel without entering any information.' This confirms credential-harvesting outcome.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on authentication attempts within 5 minutes of a user session on known-affected websites (Toshiba, Muji, Zojirushi, Samsung, etc.). Flag failed authentication followed by password reset requests. Monitor user help-desk tickets mentioning unexpected login prompts during June 2026 timeframe.

suggestion.title: Widespread HTTP 401 Abuse Across Multiple Customer-Facing Domains via Single Compromised CDN
suggestion.rationale: Article describes scope: 'impacted more than 100,000 websites' and lists multiple victims: 'Toshiba and mega-retailer Muji...Zojirushi, FiNC Technologies, Ishiyaku Publishers...Hobonichi...Samsung Smart TVs.' Single point of compromise with broad impact.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify all external CDN dependencies in production applications. Create baseline of CDN domains and response codes. Alert on 401 responses from any public CDN. Correlate 401 spike across multiple internal applications originating from same external domain within a 24-hour window.

suggestion.title: Mass Injection of Malicious Code via Unowned Domain Registration Gap
suggestion.rationale: Root cause explained: 'when the domain expired, it could be claimed by anyone' and 'when the domain expired, a Chinese entity purchased it and added malicious scripts.' Governance gap in dependency domain ownership is the enabling vulnerability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Audit all third-party domain dependencies in web applications for ownership/registrant changes. Alert on domain registrant changes for CDN providers, JavaScript libraries, or stylesheet hosts. Implement HTTPS pinning and Subresource Integrity (SRI) checks on all external script/style loads to detect content drift.

suggestion.title: FFmpeg Process Spawns System Binary Post-Input Processing
suggestion.rationale: 21 FFmpeg zero-days imply active exploitation chains; processing untrusted media triggers code execution. Pipeline missed execution-phase detection for this explicit threat.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag FFmpeg (ffmpeg.exe, ffmpeg) spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or rundll32.exe within 10 seconds of processing media files from Downloads, temp directories, or network shares.

suggestion.title: Outdated FFmpeg Version Active on Endpoint
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly documents 21 zero-days in FFmpeg; unpatched versions are vulnerable. Pipeline should detect vulnerable software versions as initial-access indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Enumerate FFmpeg process version via file properties or command-line flags. Alert if version predates patch release date from security advisory.

suggestion.title: Outdated Chrome Version Active on Endpoint
suggestion.rationale: 429 Chrome patches indicate widespread exploitable surface; unpatched Chrome is high-severity initial-access risk. Pipeline should prioritize version detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor chrome.exe version via registry (HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Google\Chrome) or process properties. Alert if major version is older than current stable release minus 2 versions.

suggestion.title: Chrome Renderer Crash Followed by System Binary Spawn
suggestion.rationale: Chrome zero-days exploited via malicious web content often trigger sandbox escape + code execution. 429 patches suggest active exploitation chains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Chrome renderer process crash event or abnormal termination followed within 5 seconds by Chrome main process launching cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or system utilities outside normal user-initiated flows.

suggestion.title: FFmpeg Decoding Untrusted File + Memory Fault Pattern
suggestion.rationale: FFmpeg vulnerabilities are memory-corruption class (heap overflow, OOB read); exploited by malformed media frames. Zero-day exploitation exhibits crash + child process.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor FFmpeg opening video/audio files from risky sources (email downloads, web-based media, network shares) followed by abnormal termination or segfault equivalent, then suspicious child process launch.

suggestion.title: Malicious Website Navigation Triggers Chrome Sandbox Escape
suggestion.rationale: Chrome zero-day exploitation chains typically pivot through sandbox—article's 429 patches almost certainly include sandbox bypasses. Missing execution-phase detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate Chrome network event (visit to low-reputation domain) with Chrome spawning system binaries or loading kernel drivers outside normal sandbox constraints within 10 seconds.

suggestion.title: SolarWinds Serv-U Exploitation Attempt Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'actively exploited' — the primary threat vector is malicious actors sending exploitation payloads to Serv-U endpoints. Pipeline failed to map initial-access phase entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP(S) traffic to SolarWinds Serv-U default ports (3496, 3497) for known exploitation patterns, anomalous query strings, or error-code spikes. Correlate with CISA KEV advisory signatures and public PoC repositories. Alert on repeat attempts from single source IPs.

suggestion.title: Network-Based Denial of Service Against Serv-U Service
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies a 'DoS Flaw' — the vulnerability's core mechanism is service disruption. Pipeline completely omitted the impact phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect volumetric anomalies targeting Serv-U listener ports: sustained packet-rate or connection-rate increases, SYN-flood fingerprints, UDP amplification, or HTTP flooding. Establish baseline per host and alert on 300%+ spike. Correlate with Serv-U process resource exhaustion.

suggestion.title: Serv-U Process Termination and Restart Loops
suggestion.rationale: DoS attacks terminate service availability — the outcome of exploitation. Pipeline missed operational impact detection entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected Serv-U process exit (non-zero exit codes) or rapid restart loops outside scheduled maintenance. Alert on multiple crashes within 5-minute windows. Correlate timestamps with inbound network anomalies 30-60 seconds prior.

suggestion.title: Command and Control from Compromised Serv-U Instance
suggestion.rationale: Exploited Serv-U hosts may serve as staging points for lateral movement or exfiltration; article does not exclude secondary payload delivery.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline outbound destinations and protocols for Serv-U hosts. Alert on new external IPs, non-standard ports, or traffic to known C2 infrastructure. Cross-reference with abuse.ch feeds and threat intelligence. Investigate traffic volume anomalies 5+ minutes post-exploitation.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-20245 Exploitation Attempt Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Actively Exploited – No Patch Available'. Detection of exploitation attempts is immediate priority for unpatched critical vulnerability in active use.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP/HTTPS requests to Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager for known exploit payload patterns, suspicious parameter injection targeting documented vulnerable endpoints, or anomalous request sequences characteristic of CVE-2026-20245 exploitation.

suggestion.title: Unexpected Process Execution from SD-WAN Manager Service
suggestion.rationale: Active exploitation implies command execution capability; attacker will spawn child processes to enumerate, persist, or move laterally.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on child process creation from Cisco SD-WAN Manager service processes launching cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, or system utilities (net.exe, ipconfig, whoami) inconsistent with normal operations.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Outbound Connectivity from SD-WAN Manager
suggestion.rationale: Post-exploitation, attacker uses compromised manager (network-privileged position) for C2 or lateral movement setup. Article's active-exploitation status implies attacker foothold persistence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag outbound connections from SD-WAN Manager to non-whitelisted external IPs, non-standard ports (especially 443/8443 to non-standard destinations), or traffic patterns consistent with C2 beaconing.

suggestion.title: Suspicious File or Registry Modification in SD-WAN Manager Directories
suggestion.rationale: Persistence without patch requires attacker to modify configuration, install backdoors, or establish autostart mechanisms in SD-WAN Manager file system or registry.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor creation/modification of executable files or scripts in Cisco SD-WAN Manager installation directories, or unauthorized changes to service/startup registry keys or config files.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement from SD-WAN Manager to Internal Targets
suggestion.rationale: SD-WAN Manager has broad network access; post-exploitation, attacker pivots to internal systems.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on authentication attempts (failed or successful RDP, SSH, Kerberos) originating from SD-WAN Manager to internal targets, especially to domain controllers or sensitive systems previously uncontacted by this host.

suggestion.title: WordPress Admin Account Creation via eval() Injection
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'The attacker submits a value for a text field that begins with a single quote to close the wrapping string literal, followed by a PHP statement that calls wp_insert_user() to create a new administrator account with the username diksimarina.' Direct persistence indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on new WordPress admin-role accounts created outside maintenance windows. Cross-reference with form submission timestamps. Monitor database logs for wp_insert_user() calls with 'role' parameter set to 'administrator' correlated with Everest Forms POST requests.

suggestion.title: PHP Single-Quote Injection in Form Fields
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'an attacker can close the intended string, inject arbitrary PHP code, and comment out the remaining generated code to achieve code execution.' Technique: quote-escape to break PHP eval() context, inject arbitrary statements, comment out remainder with //.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect POST requests to /wp-content/plugins/everest-forms with form field payloads containing single quotes followed by PHP keywords (wp_insert_user, base64_decode, system, eval). Flag payloads ending with // comment marker. Monitor for 500/parse errors in PHP logs correlating with such requests.

suggestion.title: Traffic from Known Exploitation IP Addresses
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'exploitation attempts originate primarily from two IP addresses, 202.56.2[.]126 and 209.146.60.26' with recommendation to 'block them.' Over 29,300 blocking attempts documented by Wordfence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Block and alert on any traffic from 202.56.2[.]126 or 209.146.60.26 to WordPress instances. Retroactively hunt for successful requests from these IPs in April 2026 onwards. Review access logs for successful form submissions (HTTP 200) from these IPs without corresponding error logs.

suggestion.title: Detection of Unpatched Everest Forms Pro Installations
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies CVE-2026-3300 affects 'versions 1.9.12 and earlier.' Patch released March 18, 2026. Exploitation began April 13, 2026—providing 26-day window where patched vs. unpatched status determined vulnerability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan WordPress /wp-content/plugins/everest-forms/readme.txt or version.php for version number. Alert if version <= 1.9.12 detected. Cross-reference against patched version 1.9.13+ to identify systems requiring immediate patching.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Admin Account Hunting (diksimarina Pattern)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly recommends: 'review log files and administrator accounts for any suspicious activity, especially containing the string "diksimarina."' Direct IOC for post-compromise forensics.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query wp_users table for accounts with username containing 'diksimarina' or created between April 13–present with admin role. Check user meta for IP address, creation method. Inspect WordPress action hooks for user creation events lacking normal administrative action logs.

suggestion.title: Wordfence Firewall Block Spike Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Telemetry data from Wordfence firewall and malware scanner for WordPress shows that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild' with 'over 29,300 attempts.' Exploitation volume provides behavioral signature.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Wordfence logs for spike in 'blocked' CVE-2026-3300 signatures on Everest Forms form endpoints. Alert if block count exceeds baseline by >5x. Correlate with access logs to identify requests that bypass Wordfence (false negatives). Identify source IP distribution.

suggestion.title: Smart TV Excessive Outbound HTTPS Requests
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states smart TVs are being 'turned into web-scraping proxies'—implies high-volume HTTP/HTTPS requests to external sites. No detection logic was surfaced.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline outbound HTTPS connections per TV device per hour. Flag when a single TV initiates >100 unique destination IPs in 1h window or >1000 requests in 4h. Scraping payloads often repeat User-Agent and HTTP methods (GET heavy, minimal variance).

suggestion.title: Suspicious App Installation on Smart TV
suggestion.rationale: Article describes threat vector as 'free apps'—installation is initial access. Pipeline missed the persistence/installation angle entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor installation of apps from untrusted sources or apps without prior device history. Flag side-loading attempts, apps granted network+system permissions, or installs from third-party marketplaces outside official store.

suggestion.title: Unusual Bandwidth Consumption from IoT Device
suggestion.rationale: Web scraping at scale consumes significant bandwidth. Article implies large-scale data exfiltration ('quietly turning' devices suggests persistent, high-volume activity).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish per-device baseline egress bytes. Flag when TV device exceeds typical usage by >5x or consumes >10 GB/day. Scraping traffic has high byte-to-connection ratio and sustained traffic patterns.

suggestion.title: App-Initiated Outbound Traffic from Smart TV to Non-CDN Domains
suggestion.rationale: Compromised apps phone home to C2 or scraping aggregator infrastructure. No domains or C2 patterns were identified by pipeline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Map apps to their expected egress destinations. Flag connections to non-whitelisted domains originating from app context. Correlate with known botnet-related domains or residential proxy services (e.g., beacon patterns, retry intervals).

suggestion.title: Smart TV Process Execution: Unexpected Resource Consumption
suggestion.rationale: Scraping payload execution will show elevated CPU/memory. Article implies background app activity ('quietly'). Pipeline did not surface process-level detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor app-spawned processes for unusual subprocess chains, elevated CPU% for non-video apps, or memory growth over time. Scraping engines often spawn workers; flag forking patterns atypical for streaming apps.

suggestion.title: Auto-Start Persistence Mechanism on Smart TV App
suggestion.rationale: For scraping proxy to persist across reboots, app must auto-start. Article describes 'quietly' implies long-term persistence. Kill chain missing persistence phase entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor app auto-start registrations in TV OS (Android TV, webOS, Tizen, etc.). Flag apps that add themselves to boot-time execution without explicit user consent or system app status.

suggestion.title: Outbound Connections to Bright Data/Luminati Proxy C2 Domains
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names devices 'enrolled into a commercial residential proxy network' communicating with specific C2 domains (proxyjs.brdtnet.com, proxyjs.luminatinet.com, clientsdk.bright-sdk.com, etc.). Core attack vector and primary detection surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on outbound connections from SmartTV devices (identified by MAC OUI or device metadata) to known Bright Data/Luminati proxy domains. Baseline legitimate SDK usage and flag anomalous communication patterns. Correlate timing with app installation to identify recent enrollment.

suggestion.title: Bulk Data Exfiltration from Residential SmartTV Devices to Proxy Network
suggestion.rationale: Article states apps 'scrape web data for AI training all through a consent dialog'—this manifests as sustained, high-volume outbound HTTP requests from a residential device to external hosts via proxy infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect SmartTV devices exhibiting anomalous outbound HTTP/HTTPS patterns: high request volume, requests to many external domains, low correlation with user interaction events. Flag bulk transfers to proxy infrastructure that deviate from normal television usage profiles.

suggestion.title: SmartTV App Installation with Obfuscated Network Permissions
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes apps hide consent: 'consent dialog buried in a TV remote's arrow-key navigation.' Apps request network access permissions but obscure them from users through UX deception.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor SmartTV app installs from official app stores (Samsung, LG, Roku). Flag apps requesting broad network permissions from unverified publishers, especially those added or modified in recent versions. Cross-reference app package signatures against known malicious app lists.

suggestion.title: Persistent SmartTV Device Enrollment in Commercial Proxy Network
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'millions of living room devices' persistently enrolled in proxy network. Devices maintain long-lived C2 registration and periodically check in for tasking.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline of SmartTV outbound connections to proxy infrastructure. Alert on devices establishing recurring, time-based communication to C2 domains over extended periods (days/weeks). Distinguish from legitimate Luminati SDK presence by device class, connection frequency, and payload patterns.

suggestion.title: Malicious Commits to High-Value Repositories
suggestion.rationale: Article states the worm hit '73 Microsoft GitHub Repositories'—this is a supply chain attack via code injection. Detection should identify commits with embedded payloads, suspicious file additions, or obfuscated changes to trusted repos.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect commits to Microsoft-owned repositories that introduce executable code, compressed/encoded content, or files not typical of the project's language/tooling. Correlate commit author reputation, IP geolocation, and time-of-day anomalies.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Repository Access or Mass Cloning
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attack on 73 repos suggests either mass reconnaissance or compromise of an account with broad access. Article implies coordinated targeting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag rapid enumeration of repository metadata (names, branches, committer history) from a single source IP or session. Alert on bulk cloning of repos not typically accessed by that user/service account.

suggestion.title: Worm Distribution / Malware Staging via Code Artifacts
suggestion.rationale: Named threat 'Miasma Worm' suggests an active malware family. Detection should identify binary artifacts, build outputs, or release assets that contain known Miasma signatures or suspicious PE/script files.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor GitHub release artifacts, compiled binaries, and build outputs for signatures matching known Miasma samples. Correlate with endpoint telemetry showing execution of code pulled from affected repos.

suggestion.title: Cross-Repository Supply Chain Compromise (Dependency Injection)
suggestion.rationale: If worm affects multiple repos including foundational libraries/SDKs, downstream consumers could be compromised. Article scale (73 repos) suggests potential for wide blast radius.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify deployed artifacts (NuGet, npm, Maven packages) built from compromised Microsoft repos. Track dependent projects and flag applications pulling from affected versions.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Compromise - GitHub Actions / Azure Functions
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'supply chain attack targeting AI coding agents' with Azure Functions Action explicitly disabled. No detection for compromised upstream Actions or Functions deployments.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor GitHub Actions marketplace and Azure Functions deployments for unexpected version releases, ownership changes, or code injection from previously-stable publishers. Flag commits modifying workflow triggers or secrets access without corresponding pull request reviews.

suggestion.title: Malicious GitHub Actions Workflow Execution - Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Article states '72 other repositories disabled after' attack; implies mass exploitation via compromised workflows. No UC for secrets exfiltration or lateral movement through CI/CD.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on GitHub Actions jobs that transmit secrets, environment variables, or source code to external URLs; detect unusual curl/wget/Invoke-WebRequest calls within workflow logs pointing to attacker C2 infrastructure; correlate with new self-hosted runner registrations.

suggestion.title: Repository Bulk Disable / Access Revocation Post-Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article: '72 other repositories disabled.' No UC to detect post-breach containment actions or mass defensive repository quarantine.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate bulk repository disablement, branch protection removals, or visibility changes (private→public or vice versa) with prior security events: failed auth attempts, unusual Actions logs, secrets rotations, or threat notifications. Track organization admin actions within hours of IOC publication.

suggestion.title: AI / ML Coding Agent Credential Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Title: 'targeting AI coding agents.' No detection for when autonomous agents or bot service accounts are weaponized to commit malicious code or modify CI/CD pipelines.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline AI agent service account behavior (commit patterns, repos touched, frequency). Alert on deviations: commits to unfamiliar repos, workflow modifications outside approved templates, code introducing known signatures or suspicious downloads during agent job execution.

suggestion.title: Azure Functions Deployment from Compromised GitHub Actions
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Azure Functions Action... disabled.' No specific detection for unauthorized serverless code injection via hijacked CI/CD.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Azure Functions deployments triggered by GitHub Actions for: new/modified runtime handlers, unexpected execution identities, code commits outside change windows, or suspicious ingestion of credentials during deployment.

suggestion.title: Miasma Worm - Known Signature Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title names threat: 'Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again.' No IOC extraction for malware hashes, signatures, or behavioral patterns despite named actor.
